summary:
Lunar-tic is an interactive web app for specialists and non-specialists to compare lunar locations and landing dates, including a reference point near the Moon's South Pole. Using NASA/JPL Horizons data, it visualizes Sun and Earth positions and estimates their visibility during a selected surface activity.

The project addresses a practical challenge in lunar exploration: understanding how a change in landing date affects the geometry behind solar power potential and direct-to-Earth communication. Users choose from a range of preset locations and compare alternatives against an original scenario, with results ranked by their chosen priorities.

A 3D Moon overview and local horizon view share a timeline, with explanations and numerical results for different levels of experience. Lunar-tic brings the comparison into one browser workflow for learning and preliminary planning. Estimates use hourly Sun and Earth center positions relative to a smooth lunar reference horizon.
details:
Lunar-tic is an interactive web app that helps specialists and non-specialists compare lunar locations and landing dates through changes in Sun and Earth visibility. It brings NASA/JPL Horizons predictions, coordinated 3D views and scenario comparisons into one browser workflow for education and preliminary planning.

What does it do, and how does it work?

A landing location and its timing need to be considered together. A schedule change can alter how long the Sun and Earth remain above the local horizon during a surface activity. Lunar-tic lets users explore those changes and reconsider their original plan.

The workflow has six parts:

  1. Choose a location and activity. Users select a preset associated with Apollo 11, Apollo 17, Odysseus or Chang'e 4, or a reference point near the Moon's South Pole. They set a primary landing time, earliest and latest allowed landing dates, and activity duration. The polar reference is clearly distinguished from an actual mission landing site.
  2. Read the NASA data. The app uses bundled hourly NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides, which are predictions of celestial positions. These provide the Sun and Earth directions as seen from each supported lunar location. UTC keeps dates and times consistent throughout the comparison.
  3. Explore the views together. The 3D Moon overview places the selected location in context, while the local horizon view shows the direction and elevation of the Sun and Earth. A shared timeline connects the scene, elevation chart and numerical readings, so users can follow the same moment across the views.
  4. Inspect visibility estimates. The app estimates how long the Sun is above the reference horizon, how long Earth is above it, and how long both are above it together. Additional metrics include minimum elevations and the longest estimated intervals below the horizon. These help users examine interruptions as well as total visibility time.
  5. Compare alternatives. Users can inspect an alternative manually or request suggestions within their allowed landing dates. They order priorities such as more Sun visibility, more Earth visibility, more overlap or a smaller change from the original date. The first priority leads the ranking, with later priorities breaking ties.
  6. Keep the comparison. Inspecting an alternative preserves the original scenario. Users can retain preferred alternatives, save their plan in the current browser and download a readable text summary containing their choices, results, sources and modelling assumptions. If revised dates exclude the original scenario, it remains visible with an explicit status.

What benefits does it have?

Lunar-tic keeps the question, visual evidence and comparison results together. Users can change a location or date and inspect the consequences without separately interpreting ephemeris tables.

For non-specialists, optional explanations and the local horizon view provide a way to connect numerical results with a visible Sun or Earth position. Specialists can inspect the underlying metrics and priority order when discussing preliminary options. Both audiences work with the same data and calculations.

The preserved original scenario gives each alternative a clear point of comparison. Local saving supports returning to a plan, while the downloaded summary provides a record that can be shared for discussion.

What is the intended impact?

The project aims to make the relationship between lunar landing schedules, solar power potential and direct-to-Earth communication easier to understand. Sun and Earth visibility give users a starting point for exploring those planning concerns.

For students, educators and the public, Lunar-tic is intended to support questions such as why the same location can produce different results at different times. For specialists, it provides a common visual reference for preliminary scenario comparison and explaining trade-offs to a wider audience.

What tools, languages and software were used?

  • React and TypeScript structure the interface, inputs and application state.
  • Three.js renders the Moon overview and local horizon views.
  • Vite supports development and production builds.
  • Python retrieves and checks the NASA/JPL Horizons data used by the app.
  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio's CGI Moon Kit imagery provides the Moon colour texture for visual orientation.

How is the project creative?

Lunar-tic organizes the experience around a practical question: what changes when a landing plan changes? The original scenario remains available while users inspect other possibilities, making a schedule adjustment part of the comparison.

The global Moon view and local sky perspective explain the same scenario at different scales. User-ordered priorities also make the reason for a ranking explicit. A user interested in Sun visibility can explore a different ordering from someone prioritizing Earth visibility or a smaller schedule change.

What factors were considered?

Scientific interpretation guided the data and wording. Visibility uses apparent Sun and Earth center positions relative to a local horizontal plane on a smooth lunar reference sphere. Elevation changes are treated as linear between hourly samples when estimating durations. The outputs describe visibility geometry for education and preliminary comparison.

Data coverage also shapes the workflow. A complete activity must fit within the available predictions, and results depend on the supported locations and evaluated start times. Rankings reflect those candidates and the user's selected priorities.

The interface provides optional guidance alongside numerical detail for different levels of experience. Plan saving is explicitly local to the current browser, and the downloadable summary carries the inputs and assumptions needed to interpret the results.
